Ottawa (Odawa)

Explore Ottawa/Odawa histories through the Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s own account and the Little Traverse Bay Bands’ selected Waganakising history. These distinct community scopes matter. A selected first-person passage by Odawa author Andrew J. Blackbird provides another attributed historical voice.

Start reading here

A wider Ottawa/Odawa reading route across specifically named communities and authors; it is not one government or a universal account.

  1. Ottawa History — Adawe Cultural Center

    Begin with the Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s short, specifically scoped account.

  2. Our Land and Culture: A 200 Year History of Our Land Use

    Read the selected pages of the community-published Waganakising history, retaining the November 2005 date.

  3. History of the Ottawa and Chippewa Indians of Michigan (1887), selected Tittabawassee passage

    Compare Blackbird’s selected first-person historical recollection; the rest of his book remains outside the reviewed scope.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and context

Odawa is a community name used alongside Ottawa. Distinct Odawa nations and communities have different histories.

Read the sources [1] heritage.ottawatribe.gov

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Anishinaabe relationships, language, homelands and individual governments. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] heritage.ottawatribe.gov [2] odawa-scouting.ca [3] ottawatribe.gov

03

Begin with distinct community accounts

The Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma describes its own wider Anishinaabe relationship and homelands. The 2005 Little Traverse Bay Bands publication limits its later account to Waganakising bands, including Beaver Islands. Read their differences as part of the history.

Read the sources [4] Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma, Adawe Cultural Center and Museum [6] Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians

04

A named historical author

The selected Blackbird passage recalls travel and hospitality at a Tittabawassee riverside camp. The portrait identifies that author; his retrospective account is one voice and is not a census of river communities or a present-government record.

Read the sources [7] Andrew J. Blackbird; University of Wisconsin–Madison-hosted transcription

Ottawa History — Adawe Cultural Center ↗

The Tribe identifies itself as a sovereign nation within wider Anishinaabe peoplehood and describes Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, Kansas and Oklahoma connections. This short account is one nation’s perspective, not a universal Odawa chronology.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual About Us and Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma paragraphs, web lines 16–21 read. Linked histories, artifacts, classes and treaties were not reviewed.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Community-published historical book with elder interviewsLittle Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa IndiansSource 6

Our Land and Culture: A 200 Year History of Our Land Use ↗

Publication: November 2005; cover says compiled and printed then, not the 2021 upload date

A tribal project combining documents and elder interviews, with youth participation. Its own introduction limits later history to Waganakising bands, including Beaver Islands, and distinguishes shared identity from specific belonging. Selected pages only; neither a full-book review nor current legal interpretation. Historical vocabulary and family records are not replicated.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Visually inspected cover, contents, illustrations list, introduction printed 4–6, acknowledgements 7, chapter opening 29, and summary 43–44 (PDF 1–8,33–36,55–56, including intervening illustrations).

Review recorded: October 21, 2026

https://ltbbodawa-nsn.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Our-Land-and-Culture-for-web.pdf

Indigenous-authored primary accountAndrew J. Blackbird; University of Wisconsin–Madison-hosted transcriptionSource 7

History of the Ottawa and Chippewa Indians of Michigan (1887), selected Tittabawassee passage ↗

Blackbird’s first-person recollection describes winter travel and hospitality at a Tittabawassee riverside camp. It is a named Odawa author’s retrospective account, not an ethnic census of every camp.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Title/front matter and selected citizenship-journey passage on PDF pages 42–43, marked printed pages 60–61, read. The rest of the 140-page PDF and its language material were not reviewed for this entry.

Review recorded: October 25, 2026
